tool_args.old_string:
Running the 008d configuration (trained $\dt$-embedding, subsampling ON, $H{=}8$) with two independent seeds and an extended replication produces three qualitatively distinct outcomes (Table~\ref{tab:post_civo}).  Seed 0 exhibits full collapse: $\nve$ sustains above $1.5\times$ from 25K onward, value rises $+130\%$, and evaluation declines monotonically to 82.8.  Seed 2 exhibits transient CIVO: $\nve$ reaches $1.62\times$ at 45K (35K+ window) but the value function self-corrects to $0.38\times$ by 105K, with evaluation recovering to 267.9.  The extended replication (seed 1, 009e) shows oscillatory degradation: evaluation swings from 82.7 (55K) to 250 (65K) before declining to 131.1 at 105K, while the value function initially rises (138$\rightarrow$190 through 75K) then reverses (163$\rightarrow$135 by 105K), producing a fluctuating $\nve$ trajectory (final 1.57$\times$).

All runs cross the $\nve > 1.5\times$ threshold---CIVO triggers deterministically---yet the downstream damage is stochastic.  We hypothesize that the divergence relates to the critic's representational capacity at the time of CIVO onset.  \citet{lyle2022capacity} demonstrate that deep RL networks suffer progressive capacity loss during training, in which early-learned features become increasingly difficult to overwrite.  If the critic's capacity is already partially consumed by the time CIVO injects overestimation, the network cannot recalibrate, producing the permanent collapse of seed 0.  If sufficient capacity remains, the critic can absorb the transient overestimation and recover, as in seed 2.

The oscillatory pattern of seed 1 (009e) is particularly informative.  Through 75K, the value function rises while evaluation oscillates; after 75K, the value function declines monotonically (190$\rightarrow$135), while evaluation oscillates further (178$\rightarrow$202$\rightarrow$133$\rightarrow$131) before settling near the collapse level, indicating that the critic has lost calibration with respect to the true value landscape.  The evaluation oscillation itself likely reflects the actor alternating between exploitation of overestimated regions and exploration driven by entropy regularization.  Unlike seed 0's monotonic decline (entropy decreasing), seed 1's entropy remains elevated, suggesting the actor has not fully committed to the overestimated policy but cannot escape it either.  This intermediate state---persistent overestimation without convergent collapse---may represent a regime in which partial capacity loss allows the critic to respond to new data without being able to fully correct its biases.

tool_args.old_string: \citet{nhu2025tawm} demonstrate that $\dt$-conditioning is beneficial in the MPC framework of TD-MPC2, raising the question of why the same technique fails in DreamerV3.  The critical architectural difference lies in how the value function interacts with the world model.  In MPC, the agent re-plans from real states at every environment step, using the world model only for short-horizon action selection via sampling-based optimization.  Imagination errors do not accumulate into the training signal because there is no critic bootstrapping from imagined trajectories---the value function, if used at all, serves as a terminal cost estimate and is trained on real transitions.  In DreamerV3, by contrast, the actor-critic is trained \emph{entirely} within imagination.  The critic's value estimates feed back into actor training across full $H$-step rollouts, and any systematic reward-prediction bias at $\dt > 1$ is amplified through this closed loop.  In terms of the two-stage decomposition (\S\ref{sec:civo_mechanism}), MPC is immune because Stage~2 cannot occur: without actor-critic bootstrapping from imagined trajectories, there is no mechanism for the actor to exploit the dynamics bias.  The feedback architecture---not the temporal conditioning itself---is what transforms a manageable model imprecision into a pathological training signal.  This distinction aligns with \citet{frauenknecht2025rollouts}, who find that rollout quality is a dominant factor in model-based RL performance, and with the time-discretization analysis of \citet{tallec2019making}, who show that temporal resolution mismatches can destabilize value learning in model-free settings.

The CIVO mechanism identifies a structural incompatibility between flat temporal conditioning and imagination-based actor-critic training.  The RSSM, designed for single-scale dynamics, cannot maintain prediction fidelity across temporal resolutions when conditioned via a learned embedding---the co-adaptation between embedding and reward head produces the asymmetric errors that drive the feedback loop.  Hierarchical approaches that abstract temporal scales at the representation level, such as THICK \citep{gumbsch2024thick}, Hieros \citep{mattes2024hieros}, and LS-Imagine \citep{li2025lsimagine}, may avoid this failure mode by maintaining separate dynamics models for each temporal scale rather than conditioning a single model on $\dt$.

DreamerV4 \citep{hafner2025dreamerv4} replaces the RSSM with a transformer architecture, raising the question of whether CIVO transfers to attention-based world models.  The transformer's capacity for in-context temporal reasoning could either mitigate the asymmetric fidelity problem---by better modeling multi-scale dynamics within a single architecture---or amplify it, if attention weights co-adapt with the temporal embedding in a manner analogous to the RSSM's reward head.  Resolving this question requires extending the present diagnostic framework to transformer-based world models.

More broadly, regularization of the $\dt$-embedding (\eg, gradient stopping to prevent co-adaptation with the reward head, or spectral normalization on the embedding weights) could potentially preserve the temporal signal's benefits for world-model training while preventing the asymmetric reward-prediction bias that initiates CIVO.  We leave empirical evaluation of such approaches to future work.
